title: Udayana Argues for God
hookLine: a logician stands at the shut doors of a great temple and reminds the Lord who defended him
carry: nyaya reasons toward god, step by step, out loud
tomorrow: is every argument just people trying to win?

lines: YOUR CASE WAS IN MY HANDS.
cards: About a thousand years ago, in Mithila in north India, a Nyaya teacher named Udayana became well-known for arguing for God, against sharp critics who said no maker of the world could ever be proved.
A story told about him has him arriving at the great Jagannath temple in Puri and finding the doors shut.
And Udayana, the story goes, speaks to the Lord, half scolding, half smiling: you ignore me now, but when the doubters came, your case was in my hands.

teach.b: His case was built with Nyaya's best-known tool, the argument in five parts. The Nyaya Sutra names them: the proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion.

teach.h: SOUND DOESN'T LAST, LIKE A POT.
teach.b: Its early commentator Vatsyayana walks them through with sound: sound does not last, because it is produced; whatever is produced does not last, like a clay pot; sound is produced; so sound does not last.
Udayana used that same frame for the biggest question of all.

teach.h: THE WORLD HAS A MAKER, LIKE A POT.
teach.b: One: the earth and things like it have a maker. Two: because they are effects, put together from parts. Three: whatever is put together has a maker, like a pot and its potter.

Four: the earth is put together. Five: so it has a maker, and Nyaya calls that maker Ishvara, the Lord. That's a real Hindu teaching: for Nyaya, God isn't only believed in; God can be reasoned toward.
And because every step is said out loud, the other side can test it. Many did.

Buddhist thinkers pushed hard on step three: is the world really like a pot? Not every Hindu school agreed either; Mimamsa thinkers saw no need for a maker of the world. Nyaya's answer wasn't to shout louder.
It was to lay out the steps, so the disagreement could land where it really lived.
So when a friend asks you to prove God, you don't have to choose between a shrug and a fight. You can say: some Hindus tried, in five steps. Here's the step people argue about.

how: In traditional Sanskrit schools, students meet Nyaya through the Nyaya Sutra and its commentaries, learning to set out an argument step by step and to test it in discussion with a teacher.

o: the school of logic: claims laid out in checkable steps, even about God
a code of law that courts use to settle disputes
the art of winning any debate with clever words

games.q: the five-part argument — tap the pairs.
p: like a pot and its potter
the Lord: for Nyaya, the world's maker

s: in Nyaya, an argument is something you work out alone in your head
the five parts are said out loud, so another person can check each step.
Udayana argued that the world has a maker, like a pot
what is put together from parts points to a maker; Nyaya calls that maker Ishvara.
every Hindu school agreed there is a maker of the world
Mimamsa thinkers saw no need for one, and argued it with Nyaya.

games.q: a friend says 'you can't argue about God, it's just faith.' you're thinking like a Nyaya teacher. what do you do?
o: shrug; nobody can reason about God.
lay out the five steps and ask which one they doubt.
say that God exists, louder, until they drop it.
games.why: Nyaya reasons toward Ishvara out loud, step by step, so the disagreement lands on the one step where it really lives.

practice: Listen to one sound, a chime if you have one, or whatever comes next, and follow it all the way down into quiet.
Then hold up one rule of thumb you live by, like anyone who's late doesn't care, and look for its pot: one real case where it plainly held, and one where it didn't.
If you pray, you can rest in the name of God you use as the silence settles.

wordCard.voice: Nyaya. The school of logic, and its argument in five parts, which Udayana used to reason toward Ishvara, the Lord.

orig.note: Sanskrit: nyaya, the name of the school of logic and reasoning.
